headline: Federal Supervised-Release Rate Fell to 82% in Fiscal 2025
dek: The Sentencing Commission counted 50,688 prison sentences followed by supervision, down five percentage points from fiscal 2021.
entities: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts

sources.title: Supervised Release Quick Facts, Fiscal Year 2025

lead.creator: Carol M. Highsmith
lead.rightsBasis: Carol M. Highsmith dedicated this Library of Congress photograph to the public domain; Commons records no known publication restrictions.
lead.attribution: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress
lead.caption: The U.S. Courthouse in El Paso, Texas. Fiscal 2025 sentencing data show wide district variation in the use of supervised release after imprisonment.
lead.alt: Exterior of the federal courthouse in El Paso at dusk.

charts.caption: Of 61,557 fiscal 2025 sentences that included imprisonment, 50,688 also included supervised release.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 61,557 prison sentences and 50,688 terms of supervised release, an 82 percent rate.

charts.caption: Two-thirds of 53,087 post-conviction supervision cases closed without revocation; one-third closed with revocation.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 66 percent of supervision cases closed without revocation and 34 percent with revocation.

paragraphs: Federal judges imposed supervised release after 82% of prison sentences in fiscal year 2025, according to the United States Sentencing Commission, a five-percentage-point decline from fiscal 2021.
The commission reported 66,662 federal cases for the year. Of those, 61,557 sentences included imprisonment, and 50,688 of the prison sentences also included a term of supervised release.

Supervised release is a court-ordered period after imprisonment, distinct from probation. The fiscal 2025 figures describe sentences and supervision records, not a measure of future offending or individual risk.

The average supervision term was 46 months after an average prison term of 61 months. Ninety-two percent of imposed terms fell within the range set by the guideline policy statement in section 5D1.2(a).

A statute required supervision in 22% of the cases in which it was imposed. The commission excluded cases with incomplete sentencing information and 23 supervision terms that were not paired with imprisonment from its headline calculation.

District rates varied substantially. Eight districts imposed supervision after every prison sentence in the dataset, while the five lowest rates ranged from 39% in New Mexico to 63% in the Middle District of Louisiana.

Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts data incorporated by the commission counted 119,532 people under federal post-conviction supervision on September 30, 2025. Ninety percent were on supervised release and 9% were on probation.
Among 53,087 supervision cases closed during the year, 66% closed without revocation and 34% closed with revocation. The commission said 23% of all closures followed a technical violation.

The commission also noted that a guideline amendment to its supervised-release policy statement took effect November 1, 2025. The fiscal 2025 statistics mostly describe sentences imposed before that change and should not be read as an evaluation of the amendment.
facts: The commission reported 61,557 fiscal 2025 sentences that included imprisonment.
Supervised release accompanied 50,688 of those sentences, or 82%.
The average supervision term was 46 months.
Of 53,087 supervision cases closed, 66% closed without revocation.
uncertainty: The commission labels the Quick Facts release June 2026 but does not display a day; the citation date preserves month-level precision at the start of that month.
Cases with incomplete sentencing information were excluded, and the figures do not predict individual outcomes.
seoTitle: Federal supervised release rate fell to 82% in FY2025
seoDescription: USSC data show supervised release followed 50,688 federal prison sentences in fiscal 2025, an 82% rate.

headline: Four Agencies Have Not Fully Met New Strategic-Review Rules, GAO Says
dek: OMB guidance omitted four leadership and stakeholder requirements, and none of the selected agencies had fully implemented the 2024 law.

sources.title: Government Performance Management: OMB and Selected Agencies Need to Fully Address New Requirements

lead.creator: Daderot
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer released the work under the CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Eisenhower Executive Office Building houses the Office of Management and Budget. GAO says OMB guidance did not fully communicate new strategic-review requirements.
lead.alt: Ornate stone facade of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington.

charts.caption: GAO found that none of four selected agencies had fully implemented the new strategic-review requirements.
charts.alt: Graphic notes four selected agencies, zero with full implementation and four gaps in leadership and stakeholder requirements.

charts.caption: DHS and Treasury addressed most requirements in process documents; State and GSA had not developed comparable documents.
charts.alt: Graphic compares strategic-review documentation at DHS, Treasury, State and GSA.

paragraphs: Four federal agencies had not fully implemented new strategic-review requirements, and incomplete Office of Management and Budget guidance contributed to the gaps, the Government Accountability Office reported.

The Federal Agency Performance Act of 2024 requires agencies to assess whether organizations, programs and activities are contributing as planned to agency goals. It also directs the government to manage crosscutting work that can span multiple departments.

GAO said OMB established new cross-agency goals in December 2025 within the first year of the administration, meeting that timing requirement. But OMB's August 2025 guidance did not fully address four statutory requirements involving agency leaders and stakeholders.

GAO reviewed the Departments of Homeland Security, State and Treasury and the General Services Administration. None of the four had fully implemented the new strategic-review requirements at the time of the review.
DHS and Treasury had policies, procedures and guidance that addressed most, but not all, requirements. State and GSA had not developed comparable process documentation, according to the report.

DHS, Treasury and GSA told GAO they planned to conduct strategic reviews in 2026. State would not confirm that it planned to do so, which GAO said could deny its leadership a chance to identify risks and improve performance.

The review focused on compliance and management processes; it did not attempt to score the policy outcomes of every agency program. GAO selected four agencies from 13 included in earlier work, so its findings are not a census of the government.

GAO recommended that OMB revise its guidance, that each selected agency fully document its review process and that State conduct a strategic review in 2026. DHS, GSA, State and Treasury agreed with the relevant recommendations; OMB did not comment.

The recommendations remain the accountability mechanism to watch. Completing documents and reviews would show procedural compliance, while later evidence would still be needed to establish whether the reviews improved cross-agency results.
facts: OMB established new crosscutting goals in December 2025.
OMB guidance did not fully address four leadership and stakeholder requirements.
None of four selected agencies had fully implemented the new strategic-review requirements.
GAO issued recommendations to OMB and all four selected agencies.
uncertainty: GAO selected four agencies from a group of 13; the findings do not establish a government-wide compliance rate.
Agreement with a recommendation is not evidence that corrective action has been completed.
seoTitle: GAO finds gaps in federal strategic reviews at four agencies
seoDescription: GAO says OMB guidance and four selected agencies have not fully met Federal Agency Performance Act review rules.

headline: CBO Doubts a One-Time Wealth Tax Could Secure Social Security for 75 Years
dek: The agency compared a $30.3 trillion projected OASI shortfall with $55 trillion in top-1% wealth, warning that design and behavior would sharply reduce collections.

sources.title: Answers to Questions for the Record Following a Hearing on Social Security's Finances
2026 Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Federal Disability Insurance Trust Funds

lead.creator: Carol M. Highsmith
lead.rightsBasis: Carol M. Highsmith placed the photograph in the public domain; the Library of Congress records no known restrictions.
lead.attribution: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress
lead.caption: The Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building in Washington was originally built as the Social Security Building. CBO addressed lawmakers' questions about financing the OASI trust fund.
lead.alt: Wide exterior view of the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building in Washington.

charts.caption: CBO cited trustees' estimate of a $30.3 trillion 75-year OASI shortfall and Federal Reserve data showing $55 trillion in top-1% household wealth.
charts.alt: Graphic compares a 30.3 trillion dollar Social Security gap with 55 trillion dollars in top one percent wealth and a 2032 exhaustion date.

charts.caption: CBO said valuation, avoidance incentives and the widening long-run gap make a simple tax-rate calculation unreliable.
charts.alt: Graphic lists hard-to-value assets, behavioral responses and a widening gap after 75 years.

paragraphs: A one-time wealth tax on the richest 1% of households is highly unlikely to generate enough revenue to make Social Security's retirement trust fund solvent for 75 years, the Congressional Budget Office told senators.

CBO was responding to questions submitted after a March hearing on Social Security. The agency did not estimate a tax rate or score legislation; it explained why a simple comparison of wealth and the program's financing gap would overstate potential collections.

The Social Security trustees estimate the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance program's unfunded obligation over 75 years at $30.3 trillion. Federal Reserve data put wealth held by the top 1% at $55 trillion in the first quarter of 2026.

Those figures are not directly interchangeable. CBO said a tax broad enough to cover housing, closely held businesses and retirement accounts would be difficult to design and administer, while households would have strong incentives to reduce taxable wealth.

Behavioral responses would substantially reduce revenue relative to multiplying a headline tax rate by current wealth, CBO said. The agency also said a one-time levy large enough to pursue the target would have significant effects on the broader economy.

CBO therefore concluded that the effective rate would need to be very high and would probably still miss the 75-year goal. The agency noted that the Joint Committee on Taxation, not CBO alone, would estimate the revenue from an actual wealth-tax bill.
The answer also cautioned that 75-year balance would not guarantee lasting solvency because the projected gap between Social Security revenue and outlays widens after the projection window.

CBO projects that the OASI trust fund will be exhausted in fiscal 2032 under current law, while the Disability Insurance trust fund remains solvent for more than 30 years. Its baseline must assume scheduled benefits continue for budget projection purposes even when a trust fund lacks enough resources.

The document analyzes financing mechanics rather than endorsing a policy. Any real proposal would depend on statutory definitions, enforcement, valuation rules, taxpayer responses and broader economic effects that are not captured by the two headline dollar amounts.
facts: The trustees estimate a $30.3 trillion 75-year OASI unfunded obligation.
The Federal Reserve estimated $55 trillion in top-1% household wealth in the first quarter of 2026.
CBO projects OASI trust fund exhaustion in fiscal 2032 under current law.
CBO did not estimate a specific wealth-tax rate or score legislation.
uncertainty: The $30.3 trillion trustees' figure is a present-value estimate under intermediate assumptions and is not a current cash bill.
Actual receipts would depend on legislation, valuation, enforcement, behavioral responses and economic effects.
seoTitle: CBO doubts one-time wealth tax could secure Social Security
seoDescription: CBO says a one-time top-1% wealth tax would likely fall short of Social Security's 75-year financing gap.

headline: Prescribed Burns Made Giant Sequoias Nearly Four Times More Likely to Survive
dek: A NASA-funded analysis of 26,403 trees across 19 groves estimates earlier controlled fire saved roughly 1,800 giant sequoias in 2020 and 2021.
entities: Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks

sources.title: NASA-Funded Study Shows How Controlled Burns Help Sequoias Survive Wildfires
Prescribed fire increases giant sequoia survival under extreme wildfire

lead.creator: Anthony Caprio, National Park Service; Samuel Grinis
lead.rightsBasis: NASA published the composite as official science-news media; the documentary field photograph is credited to the National Park Service and the image is reused with full agency credit in the same scientific context.
lead.license: U.S. government/NASA editorial reuse with credited component
lead.attribution: National Park Service/Anthony Caprio; Samuel Grinis via NASA
lead.caption: Aerial evidence of sequoia mortality and survival appears beside General Sherman in NASA's study summary. Researchers linked earlier prescribed fire with much higher survival in extreme wildfire.
lead.alt: Aerial forest view showing burned sequoia habitat beside a photograph of the giant sequoia General Sherman.

charts.caption: Researchers analyzed 26,403 giant sequoias across 19 groves affected by the 2020 and 2021 fire seasons.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 26,403 giant sequoias, 19 groves and two severe fire seasons.

charts.caption: The analysis associated prescribed fire with nearly four times greater survival and estimated about 1,800 trees were saved.
charts.alt: Graphic shows nearly four times higher survival, about 1,800 trees saved and 19 percent mature-tree loss across the range.

paragraphs: Giant sequoias in forests treated with prescribed fire were nearly four times more likely to survive extreme wildfire than trees in untreated areas, according to a NASA-funded study.

Researchers analyzed 26,403 giant sequoias in 19 groves after California's 2020 and 2021 fire seasons. They combined lidar, tree-location maps, high-resolution imagery and statistical modeling to estimate mortality under different management histories.

The team estimated that prescribed burns saved roughly 1,800 giant sequoias. Those intentional, controlled fires reduce accumulated underbrush, dead wood and other fuel that can drive high-intensity wildfire.

The study focused on a period of exceptional damage. NASA said 6.8 million acres burned in California across the two fire seasons and 19% of the mature giant-sequoia population across its natural range was destroyed.
Giant sequoias naturally occur only on the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada. They can exceed 300 feet in height, 30 feet in diameter and 3,000 years in age, according to NASA's summary.
Researchers said the new evidence strengthens a practice long supported by field experience but previously lacking species-wide quantitative evaluation under extreme fire conditions.

The analysis does not mean every prescribed burn prevents later tree death. Survival depends on fire severity, treatment history, local fuels, weather and other conditions, and controlled fire itself requires planning and suitable operating windows.

The researchers used remote sensing to evaluate individual large trees across multiple groves, an approach they say could help assess management effects in other old-growth forests where field inventories alone are difficult.

The result is evidence about risk reduction, not elimination. As severe-fire conditions change, continued monitoring will be needed to test whether the estimated protection holds across future fires and different treatment intervals.
facts: The study analyzed 26,403 giant sequoias across 19 groves.
Prescribed fire was associated with nearly four times greater survival under extreme wildfire.
Researchers estimated roughly 1,800 trees were saved.
NASA reported that 19% of the mature giant-sequoia population was destroyed in the 2020 and 2021 fires.
uncertainty: The study estimates causal protection using observational management and fire data rather than a randomized experiment.
Results from 2020 and 2021 groves may not transfer unchanged to every forest, fire or treatment interval.
seoTitle: Prescribed burns raised giant sequoia survival, study finds
seoDescription: NASA-funded research links prescribed fire to nearly four times higher giant-sequoia survival in extreme wildfires.

headline: NIST's Looping Laser Mixed Metals That Usually Separate in 3D Printing
dek: The team rewrote printer controls to stir a tiny molten pool, then used synchrotron X-rays to watch the new alloy solidify in under a second.
entities: National Institute of Standards and Technology

sources.title: NIST Researchers Discover a New Way to Whisk Alloys Together With Lasers
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

sources.title: Laser stirring with elliptical scanning enables on-demand alloying in additive manufacturing

lead.creator: U.S. Department of Energy
lead.rightsBasis: The photograph was made by a Department of Energy employee in official duties and was verified on Commons as a U.S. government work.
lead.license: Public domain, U.S. Department of Energy work
lead.attribution: U.S. Department of Energy / Wikimedia Commons
lead.caption: A 2010 visit inside Argonne's Advanced Photon Source. NIST researchers used its high-brilliance X-rays to watch laser-stirred metal solidify.
lead.alt: Researchers and officials stand beside equipment inside the Advanced Photon Source.

charts.caption: A looping laser path stirred a microscopic molten pool without requiring major new printer hardware.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a looping laser scan path, no major new printer parts and solidification in under one second.

charts.caption: The team mixed RHEA-19 with a titanium alloy and verified the result with real-time X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.
charts.alt: Graphic lists RHEA-19 and titanium, synchrotron X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.

paragraphs: NIST researchers programmed a metal 3D printer's laser to trace repeated loops, stirring metals that ordinarily separate as the molten pool cools, the agency reported.

The method targets a basic additive-manufacturing problem: metals with different densities, melting points and surface tensions can segregate into weak, uneven regions instead of forming a uniform alloy.
Rather than tracing straight lines, the team made the laser draw loop-the-loops as it crossed the powder bed. That motion actively mixed the tiny molten pool while the material was being printed.

NIST said commercial printer software could not generate the needed path, so the researchers wrote new controls. The approach does not require major new printer parts, suggesting existing systems could eventually be adapted.

The test combined RHEA-19, a dense refractory high-entropy alloy, with a lighter titanium alloy. High-entropy alloys use several metals in relatively similar proportions and can be difficult to mix uniformly by conventional casting.

Verification required watching dense metal solidify in less than a second. At Argonne National Laboratory's Advanced Photon Source, the team used synchrotron X-ray diffraction to track atomic structure in real time.
Electron microscopy of the solidified material provided a second check. NIST said the measurements showed that the looping scan successfully mixed the two materials into a new alloy.

The researchers see a possible path toward on-demand alloys made from elemental or feedstock powders, reducing the need to stock a separate pre-alloyed powder for every composition and permitting graded parts without welds.

That remains a research prospect, not a production guarantee. The demonstration involved selected materials and laboratory equipment; repeatability, scale, qualification, software controls and performance testing would be required before safety-critical manufacturing use.
facts: The laser followed a looping rather than straight scan path.
The test combined RHEA-19 and a titanium alloy.
Researchers used synchrotron X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to verify mixing.
NIST said the method did not require major new printer hardware.
uncertainty: The work is a laboratory demonstration and does not establish production readiness or certification for specific components.
Performance with other alloy systems, machines and build scales requires further validation.
seoTitle: NIST looping laser mixes hard-to-combine 3D-printed alloys
seoDescription: NIST researchers used a looping laser path and synchrotron X-rays to mix metals that normally separate in 3D printing.

headline: State and Local Pension Assets Rose 8.46% to $6.49 Trillion
dek: Census data count more than 37 million participants, $315.02 billion in contributions and $418.25 billion in benefits during 2025.

sources.title: Census Bureau Releases 2025 Annual Survey of Public Pensions

lead.creator: Coolcaesar
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer released the work under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: CalPERS headquarters in Sacramento. The Census Bureau's national survey covers state and locally administered defined-benefit pension systems.
lead.alt: Modern glass-and-stone CalPERS headquarters building in Sacramento.

charts.caption: State and local pension assets increased from $5.98 trillion in 2024 to $6.49 trillion in 2025.
charts.alt: Graphic shows public pension assets rising 8.46 percent from 5.98 trillion dollars to 6.49 trillion dollars.

charts.caption: The survey counted $315.02 billion in contributions, $418.25 billion in benefit payments and more than 37 million participants.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 315.02 billion dollars in contributions, 418.25 billion dollars in benefits and more than 37 million participants.

paragraphs: State and local government pension systems held $6.49 trillion in short- and long-term assets in 2025, an 8.46% increase from $5.98 trillion a year earlier, the U.S. Census Bureau reported.

The Annual Survey of Public Pensions covers state and locally administered defined-benefit systems. Those plans promise a specified retirement benefit rather than an account balance determined only by individual contributions and investment returns.
More than 37 million people participated in the systems, including inactive employees who were no longer contributing but remained eligible for future benefits.
Total employee and government contributions reached $315.02 billion. Employees supplied 24.83% of that amount, while governments contributed 75.17% on behalf of workers.
Benefit payments totaled $418.25 billion in 2025, up 3.40% from $404.46 billion in 2024. Beneficiaries include retirees as well as eligible spouses and dependent children.

The fact that benefit payments exceeded contributions during the year does not by itself show whether systems are adequately funded. Pension plans also receive investment income and pay benefits from accumulated assets.

Likewise, the increase in assets is not the same as an improvement in funded status. Funded ratios depend on actuarial liabilities, discount-rate assumptions, benefit promises and other system-specific factors.
The Census Bureau publishes national and state statistics as well as a separate unit file with actuarial information for state and local systems, allowing comparisons beyond the headline totals.
The 2025 survey is a broad balance-sheet and cash-flow snapshot. Evaluating any individual pension system requires its own actuarial valuation, governance record and investment-risk profile.
facts: State and local pension assets totaled $6.49 trillion in 2025.
Assets increased 8.46% from $5.98 trillion in 2024.
The survey counted more than 37 million participants.
Benefit payments totaled $418.25 billion and contributions totaled $315.02 billion.
uncertainty: National asset and cash-flow totals do not establish the funded status of any individual retirement system.
The survey's participant count includes inactive workers eligible for future benefits.
seoTitle: Public pension assets rose to $6.49 trillion in 2025
seoDescription: Census data show state and local pension assets rose 8.46% to $6.49 trillion, with more than 37 million participants.
